material:
The Shelf Above the Sink

My mother offered me a shelf before she offered me a room. “You can put your bathroom things there,” she said, pointing above the sink, where an artificial fern had lived since my final year at school. The fern went on the landing. My toothbrush moved in. We managed not to discuss how long either arrangement would last.

I was forty-one and had just separated from Nerin. This is the efficient version, the one I used at work. The longer version involved six months of sleeping badly beside someone who could still make me laugh, and a last argument about whether a window should be open. I came home with two suitcases and a bag of frozen food. My mother made space for everything except the bag, which leaked on the floor.

Nine months later, I volunteered to sort the lost property at Mereglass Pool. The notice promised forty minutes every Saturday. I liked the sound of a responsibility with a number attached. At home, even buying milk had become complicated. Was I contributing to a household or being considerate during a visit? I kept my receipts, which helped nobody.

The pool's lost property lived behind reception in three plastic crates. Tessa, who ran the desk, gave me gloves and said I could throw away anything that had started growing. Everything else received a dated label and stayed for six weeks. Then clean, usable items went to the town's clothing cupboard. There was a system. I nearly thanked her for that.

On my first Saturday I found five single socks, a hairbrush, a pair of trousers with a bus ticket in the pocket, and an enormous red towel. I took the towel home to wash because it would not fit in the pool's little machine. My mother held one end while I folded it.

“Someone'll be missing that,” she said.

I imagined a family getting home and discovering its absence. An accusation in a hallway. A child saying they had definitely given it to their father. I was becoming very good at imagining households I did not have to live in.

Each week I developed favourites. There was a swimming cap with a small repair stitched through its rubber, and a purple sweatshirt whose sleeves had been shortened by folding them inward and sewing them in place. Whoever wore it would be able to grow into it again. I considered this an ingenious kindness. I put the sweatshirt at the front of the shelf.

The plain things did less well with me. A grey towel became inventory; a towel with a name was a story. I knew this was unfair even as I did it. Tessa could remember which crate held a black swimsuit without needing to invent a marriage around it. She had been doing this for eleven years.

In my fourth week, a man came looking for the red towel. I was absurdly pleased. He described the white patch near one corner where his sister had repaired it, and I fetched it with the ceremony of returning a medal.

“You must have been wondering where it got to,” I said.

“Not really. I've got another.”

I wanted him to improve his answer. He did not. He tucked the towel under his arm, thanked me and asked whether the vending machine was working. I told him it wasn't, although I hadn't checked. This remains the least defensible part of the story.

At home that afternoon, my mother asked me to move my shoes away from the back door. I heard an eviction notice. I moved them upstairs with all the injured dignity available to a person carrying three pairs of shoes.

Then I came down again and asked whether she wanted me to leave.

“I want to open the door,” she said.

We laughed, but not immediately. First there was an awkward interval in which she looked tired and I understood that she was. We had been making each other into symbols: she was shelter, I was trouble, and neither of us was allowed to be somebody trying to get a bin outside.

I still sort the crates. The purple sweatshirt went unclaimed and was collected by the clothing cupboard with everything else in its batch. I almost kept it, for reasons I could not have explained without making myself sound unbearable.

Last week I bought a hook for my dressing gown. I asked my mother where to put it, and we agreed on the back of my bedroom door. I measured badly. The hook sits a little crooked. It has not made me independent, or settled what happens next. But my dressing gown is off the chair, and the chair is available for sitting.

material:
A Reservation Is Not a Visit

Brindle Civic Workshop's new booking website made the building look busier before anyone had walked through the door. By the end of its first Monday, residents had reserved 184 sessions over the coming three weeks. A notice outside the building called this its strongest participation result in three years. The website had certainly generated activity. Whether that activity would reach the workbenches was a different question.

The workshop is publicly funded and open to residents of our district. Until last autumn, people reserved equipment by calling, visiting the desk or writing their names in a book. The replacement website was supposed to reduce the time staff spent answering the telephone. It did. According to the workshop's own January review, telephone bookings fell from an average of sixty-three a week to nine. The review also said the desk team saved about five hours each week.

Those are useful results. Anyone who has waited at the desk while a member of staff tried to spell a surname down a crackling line will understand the attraction. A resident can now book after the building closes. Staff no longer have to decipher handwriting. Nothing about these improvements requires pretending that a booking and a visit are the same thing.

The website permits each account to reserve up to four sessions a week, twenty-one days ahead. Cancelling takes a separate visit to the account page. There is no charge for failing to attend. In the first twelve weeks, reservations increased by thirty-eight per cent compared with the previous twelve weeks. Recorded arrivals increased by four per cent. These are administrative figures, not evidence of what any individual resident intended.

It is easy to make the absent residents the villains. At a council meeting in February, one speaker called them “bench hoarders”. Perhaps some people reserve casually. Perhaps a shift changes, a child is ill, or the project for which a tool was needed takes longer than expected. The workshop has not asked. We should be cautious about discovering a character defect precisely where our information runs out.

Meanwhile, a reservation that will not be used still appears to the next person as a full room. Retired cabinetmaker Sella Dorn told the council she had stopped looking at the website after finding the larger benches unavailable on three successive Thursdays. Staff later checked those dates: at least two of the six large benches were unused during each afternoon session. This does not prove Sella would have attended. It does show that the system gave her a reasonable basis for deciding not to try.

The workshop's annual funding review counts the number of residents served and the range of activities offered. Its published dashboard, however, leads with reservations. This is a small difference with consequences. When staff are praised for filling the calendar, the visible problem is an empty calendar. A full calendar containing empty benches is harder to see, especially from a council office across town.

We need three numbers where we currently emphasise one: reservations, arrivals and sessions in which someone wanted equipment but could not obtain it. The third will be imperfect. A person who closes a browser in frustration may never tell us. A short voluntary question on an unavailable session could capture some of that experience, and the desk could record unsuccessful requests made in person or by telephone. We should publish the gaps in those figures alongside the figures themselves.

Some changes could then be tried without rebuilding the website. The workshop already sends confirmation emails. It could add a cancellation link and a reminder shortly before a session. Staff could release an unclaimed station after fifteen minutes, provided residents were told that rule when booking. A small share of sessions could remain available at the desk. Each option has costs: reminders can become noise, a delayed bus can make a fair rule feel harsh, and reserved walk-in space might sit empty.

For that reason, I would start with an eight-week trial in the sewing room, where all four stations use the same booking rules and staff already record arrivals. Publish the rules before it begins. Compare use of the stations, unsuccessful requests and the time staff spend administering the room. Ask residents what changed for them. Eight weeks will not settle every seasonal question, but it should reveal whether a modest change deserves a longer test.

The workshop should keep the gains that made the website worth introducing. It should also recover the distinction that a handwritten name in a book made surprisingly easy to remember: a name is a promise, not a person at a bench. The building exists so residents can make things. Our records should help us notice when they cannot.

request: Write a 700–900 word feature for the first issue of a local general-interest magazine, using these notes.
material:
The magazine is The Rillwick Window. Its first issue appears in November. Readers are residents of the fictional town of Rillwick.

A new instrument called the Long Frame will have its first public performance at the town reading room on 16 November. It is 2.4 metres long, made from an old oak loom frame and twelve tuned metal strips. Two people play it with padded beaters. It cannot be played by one person because the working positions are too far apart.

Its makers are friends Jes Anver, a furniture repairer, and Pavi Senn, a bus dispatcher. Neither earns money from music. They began working on it in February, on Tuesday evenings in Jes's rented shed. The frame came from Pavi's aunt, who had stored it for eighteen years. She gave permission for it to be dismantled.

They built three versions. The first was too quiet for listeners across the shed. In the second, several strips struck the frame. The current version has been played for six invited neighbours. One called the sound “a cupboard full of bells”; another found it unpleasant.

Jes says, “I thought making it would be the hard bit.” Pavi says, “We spend half the rehearsal deciding whose mistake it was.”

Their first composition lasts seven minutes and has no title. Admission to the performance is free; the reading room seats forty. They have no plans to sell instruments. After the concert, the frame must return to the shed because neither maker has space at home.
